description:
Welcome to Bit2Beat! We are 5 electrical engineering students from Egypt. We're passionate about music, and 2 of us play the violin!
For our project, we aim to combine music and technology to help you listen to our home planet and immerse yourself in the data and visuals from NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) in an artistic, creative way that suits everyone!
summary: Bit2Beat turns NASA Earth data into music, so anyone, including people who are blind or have low vision, can hear how our planet changes. It plays the Earth Information Center's own resources: the challenge's visualizations (ocean currents, aerosols, night lights, lightning, forest height, carbon dioxide and more), maps from the EIC data API, satellite images, climate records and live natural events. Each number becomes a note: a higher value is a higher pitch. Pictures are read band by band, videos two samples a second, events from west to east, and scientific files (GeoTIFF, NetCDF, HDF5) become maps you can explore by sound. It is built for accessibility: full keyboard and screen-reader support, push-to-talk voice control in any language, spoken explanations of the data, live captions, and the music score as a braille file. Bitty, our guide, tells an eight-chapter story of the Earth with real data. The music can be exported in stereo, headphone 3D, 5.1, 7.1 and 7.1.4 surround. It runs in any browser, works offline with the challenge data sets, and keeps your files on your device. Data is usually only seen; Bit2Beat lets everyone listen to it.
details:
What It Does

Bit2Beat is a web app that turns Earth data into music you can follow, read and export. It has four tabs: Image (NASA pictures, satellite views and scientific maps), Video (NASA visualizations), Earth events (NASA EONET natural events and USGS earthquakes) and Data (climate records and EIC data sets). A search finds any picture, video or data set of the NASA Earth Information Center, including scientific files by type.

How It Works

Each series is scaled between its lowest and highest value, and the scaled value picks a note on a musical scale (higher value = higher note); each step is one eighth note. One "plan" holds every note, and the player, the score, the readings table, the braille score, and every export read the same plan, so what you see is exactly what you hear. Pictures are measured in perceived brightness, colour and detail, or read through their own colour bar to get real values. Videos are sampled twice a second. Events are played west to east: further north is a higher note, and a bigger event is louder. Scientific files up to 5 GB are read in the browser a few pieces at a time. "What the data says" finds the trend, the highest and lowest values, and sudden jumps. You can watch more below

Accessibility & Blind features

Every control works with the keyboard and screen readers. Voice control is push-to-talk (hold V) and works in any language. "Follow pointer" says which data set, value, and place is under the pointer. There are live captions, high contrast, a dark theme, bigger text and calmer motion, and the score can be downloaded as a braille file (BRF).

Benefits And Impacts

It makes NASA Earth science reachable for blind and low-vision people, and gives everyone a new way to notice patterns: warming, seasons, storms, pollution, the growth of cities at night. It is free, needs no installation, and works offline for the challenge datasets.

Tools & AI

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (no framework), the Web Audio API for sound and 3D audio, abcjs for the music score, and Node.js tests. It is hosted on Vercel, with small server functions for the EIC gallery and for voice control. We also used Manim to make our videos.

  • fable 5.2
  • gemini API
